The industry says the mechanism’s design is problematic: it argues that not all medicines rely on digital genetic information and that the fund may overlap with existing laws. The fund’s spokesperson said contributions may remain modest while its operating systems are completed.

content.headline: UK flu season has started early, but that does not mean it will be severe
content.shortHeadline: Early flu season does not necessarily mean a worse one
content.standfirst: Flu infections are rising earlier than usual in the UK, prompting health officials to urge eligible people to get vaccinated. Experts say the timing alone cannot predict how severe the season will be.

image.caption: Respiratory viruses are circulating earlier than usual in the UK.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are sick right now

segments.body: UK flu activity is rising earlier than usual, although rates were still relatively low when the report was published. Possible explanations include changes in circulating flu strains and the timing of the southern hemisphere season, which can influence which strains reach the UK. Scientists are still debating why respiratory viruses peak when they do.

segments.title: What an early start tells us
segments.body: An early season does not automatically mean more infections or deaths overall: last year’s flu season also began early but ended with fewer flu deaths than average. The UK Health Security Agency is urging people eligible for an NHS flu vaccine to take it up. Flu often comes on quickly and more severely than a common cold, but many other viruses can cause similar symptoms.

content.headline: Drought-tolerant crops could reshape what British farms grow
content.shortHeadline: Drought-tolerant crops could reshape UK food growing
content.standfirst: Researchers are exploring crops such as lupins, chickpeas and lablab as hotter, drier summers put pressure on familiar harvests. Their prospects in the UK still depend on testing varieties, locations and risks.

image.caption: A lupin bhaji, made with flour from a drought-tolerant crop.

sources.originalTitle: The protein-packed superfoods of the future – that you could grow in your garden

segments.body: This summer’s heat and drought damaged yields of several UK crops, including wheat, oats, barley, broccoli, peas and potatoes. A new research network is studying crops that may cope better with changing conditions, including drought-tolerant lupins and chickpeas, while researchers and chefs are testing foods made from them.

segments.title: Not a guaranteed switch
segments.body: Lupin beans can be processed into flour and are high in protein, but edible lupins are not the same as ornamental garden varieties, which need processing to remove toxins. Researchers say chickpeas still need testing to find suitable UK varieties and growing regions, and to assess pests and disease. Warmer conditions may also bring new opportunities for gardeners, though late spring frosts could still damage fruit blossoms.

content.headline: Space Force gives SpaceX access to detailed satellite-tracking data
content.shortHeadline: SpaceX gains access to sensitive US satellite-tracking data
content.standfirst: A new contract gives SpaceX access to the US military’s most precise catalogue of objects in orbit, giving the company data that can improve its tracking system. Observers warn the arrangement could affect competition and government oversight.

sources.originalTitle: US military gives Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to sensitive tracking data

segments.body: The US Space Force has given SpaceX “enhanced” access to its High Accuracy Catalog, including tracking data from military sensors, telescopes and radars. The information can track objects as small as about 10cm in low Earth orbit, more precisely than SpaceX’s own Stargaze system, which the military will also be able to use.

segments.title: Questions about oversight
segments.body: A former employee of the government’s Traffic Coordination System for Space said the deal risks making SpaceX the de facto US provider of space-traffic coordination and giving it an advantage over competitors. The data is designated controlled unclassified information and has been closely held. A former NOAA official offered a different emphasis, saying SpaceX had been responsive to safety concerns and criticising the government’s failure to establish a clear framework. SpaceX and the Space Force did not respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment.

content.headline: AI-assisted Neighbours recut raises questions about actors’ consent
content.shortHeadline: AI-assisted Neighbours recut sparks consent concerns
content.standfirst: Old Neighbours episodes featuring Margot Robbie are being turned into phone-first microdrama using AI-assisted editing. Cast members say they were not consulted, while the producer says no new scenes or performances are being generated.

image.caption: Margot Robbie as Donna Freedman, left, with Jackie Woodburne as Susan Kennedy in Neighbours.

sources.originalTitle: Neighbours is being recut into a microdrama focused on Margot Robbie – and her co-stars aren’t happy

segments.body: RoseBerry Media is using an AI-assisted production tool to re-edit two Neighbours storylines featuring Margot Robbie into around 150 minutes of vertical episodes for phones. The tool is being used to analyse the archive, edit and reframe footage; the producer, Fremantle, says it will use only previously broadcast material and that a human editor reviews the work.

segments.title: Dispute over permission
segments.body: Former cast members Stefan Dennis and Matthew Werkmeister have criticised the project, with Werkmeister saying he was concerned about his image being used without his consent and that he had not been notified about possible residual payments. Fremantle says payments will follow existing agreements. The actors’ union says it is assisting cast members, while the Australian Writers’ Guild is in discussions with Fremantle.

content.headline: Study links problematic digital-media use with health risks for young people
content.shortHeadline: Study links problematic media use to health risks for under-25s
content.standfirst: A Lancet series reviewing evidence on nine million people under 25 links problematic digital-media use with mental-health, sleep and activity concerns. The researchers say the associations are modest and call for better platform data and oversight.

image.caption: Researchers examined links between digital-media use and health among people under 25.

sources.originalTitle: Three ways social media is harming young people, according to landmark study

segments.body: A three-paper series in The Lancet reviewed research involving nine million people under 25. It found that what the researchers describe as problematic digital-media use was associated with a higher risk of mental-health problems, sleep issues and reduced exercise. The authors stressed that the links were modest and do not, by themselves, establish cause and effect.

segments.title: Calls for scrutiny
segments.body: The researchers called for technology companies to share more information about how platform features affect health, and for governments to strengthen oversight. They singled out features such as infinite scroll, autoplay and personalised recommendation feeds as design choices that warrant scrutiny. Researchers also said limited access to platform data makes independent study harder.

content.headline: UK transport regulator proposes cyan lights to identify autonomous vehicles
content.shortHeadline: UK proposal would use cyan lights to mark self-driving vehicles
content.standfirst: The US road-safety agency’s proposal would let autonomous vehicles use steady cyan lights to signal that they are driving without a human monitoring the road. The colour is suggested, not required, as regulators work on common standards.

sources.originalTitle: TechCrunch Mobility: Blue-green is the color of autonomy

segments.body: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has proposed rules specifying how autonomous vehicles could use lights to indicate that they are operating in autonomous mode without a human occupant monitoring the road. The suggested colour is cyan, visible from the front, rear and sides, and the lights would remain steady rather than flash. The proposal does not mandate their use.

content.headline: Starlink appears restored for Ukraine after restrictions on military use
content.shortHeadline: Starlink appears to be working normally again in Ukraine
content.standfirst: Ukraine’s defence minister says Starshield appears to be working normally after a 10-day period in which drones lost connectivity at higher speeds. The military is still testing the service and says it has not received an explanation for the restrictions.

sources.originalTitle: Starlink seems to be working normally again in Ukraine

segments.body: Ukraine’s defence minister, Evgeniy Khmara, said Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade satellite internet service, appeared to be working normally again. The military is still conducting tests and has not received an explanation for the restrictions, according to TechCrunch’s report.

segments.title: What changed
segments.body: For about 10 days, Ukrainian drones reportedly lost connectivity when travelling at around 100mph, leaving the military unable to control some drones and making others more vulnerable because they had to fly more slowly. TechCrunch reports that Donald Trump asked Elon Musk to restore service. Musk said Ukraine had breached Starlink’s terms of service by using it for offensive drone strikes.

content.headline: Volunteer helped Linux users install PHP security fixes during the scramble
content.shortHeadline: Volunteer developer rushed PHP fixes to Linux users
content.standfirst: Ondřej Surý, who maintains PHP packages for Debian and Ubuntu in his spare time, worked to make urgent security updates easier to install after flaws were disclosed. He says major companies should contribute more to the open-source software they rely on.

sources.originalTitle: How one man became the unsung hero of the internet during a cyber-security scramble

segments.body: When the PHP vulnerabilities triggered an international rush to patch systems, Ondřej Surý converted the fixes into installable packages for Debian and Ubuntu. He has maintained PHP packages for the two Linux distributions voluntarily for more than 20 years, alongside his paid work as a director of DNS engineering at a US non-profit.

segments.title: Who supports the infrastructure?
segments.body: Surý said he felt responsible to users who depend on his work, and that he received more than $10,000 in donations during the scramble—about a year’s worth of previous contributions. He urged major technology companies to support open-source projects they use, warning that relying on contributors without giving back could have consequences. He also said AI may mean similar security incidents arrive more often.

content.headline: AI systems may reinforce bias in predictive policing, researchers warn
content.shortHeadline: Researchers warn AI could amplify bias in policing
content.standfirst: Predictive systems trained on police records may reproduce patterns shaped by where officers have historically concentrated their attention. Researchers call for independent scrutiny, while one expert says bias can be tested and reduced rather than assumed to be inevitable.

sources.originalTitle: Police using AI risks making discrimination worse, researchers warn

segments.body: Researchers warn that crime-prediction tools can create a feedback loop: police patrol an area because records suggest more crime there, more incidents are then recorded there, and the data can reinforce the same prediction. Research inside the Los Angeles Police Department found that crime data was skewed by public visibility and disproportionate police focus on Black neighbourhoods.

segments.title: Data and oversight matter
segments.body: Researchers at New York University found that, in nine of 13 US areas they examined, predictive systems could draw on police records from periods of unlawful or biased policing. Queen Mary University of London researcher Dimitrios Kollias cautioned that bias is not inevitable, saying systems can be tested and safeguards introduced. Other researchers argue that technical fixes are not enough without independent scrutiny of how the underlying records were produced.

content.headline: Google’s AI search is cutting publishers off from reader traffic
content.shortHeadline: Google’s AI search puts publisher traffic under pressure
content.standfirst: AI-generated search summaries can answer queries without a click to the original reporting, adding pressure to an online publishing model long reliant on Google. Publishers report losses; Google says search traffic remains relatively stable.

sources.originalTitle: Google’s AI search changes upended online publishing

segments.body: Google’s AI Overviews place generated summaries above links to source pages, while AI Mode offers a chatbot-like search experience. Publishers say these features can leave readers with an answer but no reason to visit the original article. Reports cited in the gather describe traffic declines at several outlets, including losses reported by some publishers of up to 89% in click-through rates for affected searches.

segments.title: A disputed relationship
segments.body: Google’s search chief has said click volume remains relatively stable and that AI search sends users to a wider range of sites. Publishers have tried to diversify through subscriptions, newsletters and social media; some can opt out of AI search features, but say that does not resolve falling traffic. Google is testing licensing and payment arrangements with publishers, though it remains unclear whether these will repair the relationship.

content.headline: Workers in India are filming everyday tasks to train robots
content.shortHeadline: Indian workers film everyday tasks to train AI robots
content.standfirst: Companies are paying people in India to record haircuts, sewing and housework as training material for physical AI. Workers describe extra income, while a labour researcher warns that the longer-term effects on jobs remain unclear.

image.caption: Mohammed Ashim records his hands while working as a barber.

sources.originalTitle: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

segments.body: Workers in India are recording ordinary tasks—including cutting hair, stitching garments and doing household chores—with head-mounted cameras. Data companies process and sell the footage to robotics and AI firms seeking examples of how people move and handle objects in real environments. One company says it pays $5 to $10 for eight to 10 hours of recorded work.

segments.title: Consent, pay and future work
segments.body: Companies say they seek workers’ consent and blur faces, but some clients are asking for multi-camera rigs that capture more of a person and their surroundings. Workers quoted in the report describe the income as useful, while a labour researcher says it is too early to know whether the work will help people or contribute to automation that displaces them. He warns workers may have little say if machines later take over tasks they helped record.

content.headline: Journalist says AI-assisted scammer used her identity to pitch a story
content.shortHeadline: Journalist says scammer used her identity to pitch AI-written work
content.standfirst: Editors at Science published a story under Caroline Williams’s name that she says she did not write. The person who submitted it denies impersonating her, leaving a dispute over how her work and identity were used.

image.caption: Journalist Caroline Williams says a scammer used her identity.

sources.originalTitle: My identity was stolen by an AI scammer. It could happen to anyone

segments.body: Caroline Williams says she was horrified to learn that Science had published an article under her name without her having written it. The magazine says it paid $1,000 for the piece, which it later removed after editors concluded the first draft appeared to have been written using AI and included quotes copied from other online articles.

segments.title: An unresolved dispute
segments.body: The person who submitted the story told The i Paper they were a different journalist with the same name, denied impersonation and said linking to Williams’s earlier work had been a mistake. Science’s managing news editor said the pitch clearly identified itself as the UK journalist. Williams says the episode damaged her professional reputation; the journal has since changed its process for checking new writers.

content.headline: Pennsylvania law requires labels on some AI-generated advertisements
content.shortHeadline: Pennsylvania requires labels on some AI-generated ads
content.standfirst: A new state law requires disclosures on advertisements significantly modified or generated by AI. Its exceptions and subjective wording leave open questions about which ads will need a label.

sources.originalTitle: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads

segments.body: Pennsylvania has passed a law requiring an advertisement to carry a disclosure when it has been significantly modified or generated by AI. The rule applies to still images, video, audio and text, and to ads expected to run in the state even if they were created elsewhere.

segments.title: Questions about scope
segments.body: The law exempts parody, satire, commentary, criticism and content that is evidently fictional, but the report notes that terms such as “significantly modified” and “evidently fictional” are not clearly defined. It also appears to focus on synthetic content that creates a false consumer perception, leaving questions about who will decide what qualifies.

content.headline: Older songs dominate streaming as AI adds to pressure on new music
content.shortHeadline: Old songs dominate streaming as AI complicates music discovery
content.standfirst: About 60% of music streamed in the first half of 2026 was at least five years old, while new artists compete for attention. AI-generated tracks account for a small share of streams, but curators warn recommendation systems may narrow discovery.

image.caption: Zara Larsson’s 2015 song “Lush Life” remains one of the year’s biggest hits.

sources.originalTitle: Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlists

segments.body: Streaming data cited by the BBC shows older music is drawing more listening than recent releases: about 60% of plays in the first half of 2026 were songs released at least five years earlier. Deezer says AI accounts for 0.5% of streams on its platform, despite Spotify removing 75 million tracks it described as spammy.

segments.title: How listeners find new music
segments.body: Some curators worry that playlists generated from listening histories will keep recommending familiar sounds rather than introduce listeners to less commercially dominant styles. Independent musicians also say viral success for one song does not necessarily create an audience for later releases. Spotify says it has policies against impersonation and is working to filter AI-related problems; the report does not establish that AI is the main cause of the shift toward older music.
